fields.Front: What is the network core, and what are the two defining properties of packet switching in the Internet?
fields.Back:
A mesh of interconnected routers. Hosts break application messages into packets; routers forward each packet from one router to the next along the path.
1) Each packet is transmitted at the FULL link capacity R (not a fraction).
2) Store-and-forward: the entire packet must arrive at a router before it can be transmitted on the next link.

fields.Front: What does store-and-forward mean, what end-to-end delay does it give over one router, and what would the delay be if routers could forward bits as they arrived?
fields.Back:
The whole packet must be received (stored) before its first bit goes out on the next link.
One packet, two links at rate R, no propagation: source finishes at L/R, router finishes at 2L/R, so d_end-end = 2L/R.
If bits were forwarded instantly it would be only L/R, but routers must receive, store and process whole packets.

fields.Front: Numeric (slide): L = 10 Kbits, R = 100 Mbps. One-hop transmission delay?
fields.Back:
d_trans = L / R = 10,000 bits / 100,000,000 bits/s = 1 x 10^-4 s = 0.1 ms.
(Trap: not 0.1 s; keep Mbps as 10^6.)

fields.Front: Numeric: (a) a 5,000-bit packet crosses 3 links of 2 Mbps each (2 routers), negligible propagation and processing - end-to-end delay? (b) 4 packets of 8,000 bits over 3 links of 1 Mbps - when does the last bit arrive?
fields.Back:
(a) N x L / R = 3 x 5,000 / 2,000,000 = 3 x 2.5 ms = 7.5 ms. Each store-and-forward hop adds one full L/R.
(b) L/R = 8,000 / 10^6 = 8 ms; pipelined, (N + P - 1) x L/R = (3 + 4 - 1) x 8 = 48 ms, not P x N x L/R = 96 ms.

fields.Front: Give the formula for sending P packets over N store-and-forward links (rate R, L bits each) and show why 3 packets over 2 links take 4L/R, not 6L/R.
fields.Back:
Total = (N + P - 1) x L/R because transmissions pipeline.
t = L/R: packet 1 at router, source starts packet 2.
t = 2L/R: packet 1 at destination, packet 2 at router.
t = 3L/R: packet 2 delivered, packet 3 at router.
t = 4L/R: packet 3 delivered. Total 4L/R = (2 + 3 - 1) L/R.

fields.Front: When do packets queue at a router, when are they lost, and what did the slide's figure show?
fields.Back:
If the arrival rate (bps) to an output link exceeds that link's transmission rate for a period of time:
1) packets queue in the output buffer, waiting their turn (queueing delay);
2) packets are dropped (lost) if the router's buffer memory fills up.
Figure: hosts A and B send on 100 Mb/s links into a router whose outgoing link is only 1.5 Mb/s, so a queue forms.

fields.Front: Compare forwarding and routing: scope, what each does, and the time scale of each.
fields.Back:
Forwarding: LOCAL action; moves an arriving packet from the router's input link to the correct output link by looking up the destination address in the header in the local forwarding table; per packet, nanoseconds-microseconds.
Routing: GLOBAL action; routing algorithms compute source-to-destination paths, and their output populates each router's forwarding table; much slower time scale.

fields.Front: Apply: a router's forwarding table maps header values 0100, 0101, 0111, 1001 to output links 3, 2, 2, 1. A packet with destination 0111 arrives. What happens, and who built that table?
fields.Back:
The router reads destination 0111 from the packet header, finds the matching entry, and forwards the packet out link 2 (forwarding, local).
The table entries were computed by the routing algorithm (routing, global), which determines the paths packets take.

fields.Text: Store-and-forward: the {{c1::entire packet}} must arrive before transmission on the next link. Over one router (two links) the end-to-end delay is {{c1::2L/R}}; over N links it is {{c1::N x L/R}} (no propagation/processing delay).

Forwarding is a {{c1::local}} action (input link to output link via the {{c1::forwarding table}}); routing is a {{c1::global}} action in which {{c1::routing algorithms}} determine source-destination paths and fill in the forwarding tables.
